{"bodyPath":"docs/content-audits/question-quality-wave-7/coordinator-continuation-01a13294/capture-only/japan-successor-dc-alternates/shogun-history.body","bodyBytes":14795,"bodySha256":"8790a396aa0ad3bc4d00f1e849eaa69c4f855883bef1191a3b58f349364c5571","rawByteRangeHalfOpen":[5483,6561],"rawSliceBytes":1078,"rawSliceSha256":"6e579701372de0a7574d6c325f5350b9356305f40b3a170e8dccbcecf27bf4e4","normalization":"none; exact UTF-8 raw slice","literalRawSlice":"<p class=\"mb60\">The final years of the Edo period (1603–1867) were a time of unrest and social change. Under the warrior class rule of the Tokugawa shogunate, the emperor’s status had been reduced to that of figurehead. International relations with Western countries had been reestablished in 1853 after more than 260 years of near isolation, but some samurai were unhappy with the governance of shogun Tokugawa Yoshinobu (1837–1913). They were concerned that Japan’s political position would be weakened by opening up to Western nations.<br><br>\nThe Aizu domain samurai, well-known for their discipline, skills, and bravery, had close ties with the shogunate. Under the leadership of daimyo lord Matsudaira Katamori (1836–1893), Aizu sent many troops to Kyoto (the capital at the time) to help keep peace in the city. Katamori, as Yoshinobu’s cousin and trusted supporter, served as the military governor of Kyoto from 1862 to 1868.
